title: Publishers shelving tunes and then releasing them under their own names
summary: Publishers asked for submissions, put them on the shelf for years and then published them under the company's name, so people now publish their own music.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Oh, sure. You know what they used to

do? I mean, they -- like you take a -- say, for instance, you write a tune and you send it to Mills, Berlin, or any publishing house and you tell them -- like they're always saying, "Send in a tune," you know, and you send it to them and tell them to look it over.

So they'll keep it for a while and they'll send you a letter back. It says, "No, we're not interested in that kind of a tune. But leave it here, maybe a few months or something. Something might happen." It says, "We'll put it on the shelf." They'll keep that tune up there for a year and a half, two years, and wouldn't tell you nothing about it. Then they'll think you've forgot about it, and first thing you know, here comes your tune.
That publishing company's name on it. What was that tune, A Rose for a Blue Lady or something like that?
Yeah. You know how long that's supposed to be on the shelf? About five or six years. All of a sudden it comes out.
See, they're slick. They're in that business.
Well, that's why so many people have started publishing their own music, right?
That and the fact that they can collect their own royalties.

That's right. And they're better off, you know, like -- and it all depends, like, if you write a tune, say, like I wrote five now, I'm just praying I get one hit. I wouldn't care. I don't want five hits. All I want is one.
See? Then I've got mine made. I don't care about five hits. I ain't greedy. You know, but I got some pretty nice numbers on there. You haven't played yours yet, huh?
